568.title: A living sacrifice (Romans 12)
568.hook: rejoice with them that rejoice, weep with them that weep
568.howItsDone: At Mass, the priest invites the people to pray that the sacrifice, his and theirs, be acceptable to God, and Catholics speak of offering their whole day, work, joys and sufferings, as a living sacrifice, often through a morning offering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great list in Romans 8. Your line was nothing shall separate us. Which fear did you set it beside? Day five hundred sixty-eight.

Your phone buzzes twice in the same hour. One friend: we're engaged! Another: my dad's in the hospital. Two messages, two completely different rooms to walk into, and both need you. For eleven chapters, Romans has been about grace, faith and God's love. Then, in chapter twelve, Paul turns to what all that looks like on an ordinary day. And a lot of it sounds like an answer to exactly those two messages.
screen: `TWO MESSAGES IN ONE HOUR.` → `ELEVEN CHAPTERS OF GRACE.` → `THEN: WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE.`

segments.voice: Chapter twelve opens with a strange phrase. In the Douay-Rheims: "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God, your reasonable service." In Paul's world, a sacrifice was something offered at an altar, and it usually died. Paul flips it. Offer yourselves, he says, but alive. Your bodies, meaning your whole selves: your hands, your time, your Tuesday. The word translated reasonable service, logike latreia, can mean worship that fits who you are, the worship of the mind and heart. Then: don't be conformed to this world, but be made new in your mind. And then Paul gets very practical. You're one body with many members and different gifts. Let love be without pretending. Outdo one another in showing honor. Be patient in tribulation, steady in prayer. Share with the saints in need. And this: "Rejoice with them that rejoice; weep with them that weep." Notice that both halves are hard. Weeping with someone means staying in the hospital room instead of fixing things. But rejoicing with someone can be harder: being glad at a friend's engagement, with no envy in it, when one's own life seems stalled. Paul puts them side by side as one living sacrifice. The chapter ends: don't be overcome by evil, but overcome evil by good. A living sacrifice isn't a dramatic moment. It's showing up, again and again, in whichever room you're needed.
screen: `A SACRIFICE THAT STAYS ALIVE.` · `LOGIKE LATREIA: FITTING WORSHIP.` · `ONE BODY, MANY GIFTS.` · `REJOICE WITH THEM, WEEP WITH THEM.` · then, large: `OVERCOME EVIL BY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: weep or rejoice with someone. Settle, and breathe. Think of two people: one who has good news right now, and one who is hurting. Picture the first, and give gladness for them some room, with no comparing. If envy shows up, notice it kindly and set it down. Then picture the second, and stay a moment with what they're carrying, without rushing to fix it. Now choose one of them to reach out to today, a call, a message, a visit. If you pray, you can offer your body, your time and hands, as Paul says. The bell holds the time.
A living sacrifice. Offering your whole self, alive, as worship: in daily love, rejoicing with those who rejoice and weeping with those who weep. Today's word.
Your line: rejoice and weep with them. Today, walk into one person's room, glad or sad, and stay a while. Day five hundred sixty-eight.

fork.reveal: rejoice with them that rejoice; weep with them that weep. both are part of the living sacrifice.

trapdoor: what you thought: sacrifice means giving something up.
what it means: Paul asks for a sacrifice that stays alive: your whole self, offered in daily love, joy and grief shared.

569.title: The foolishness of the cross (1 Corinthians 1:18–25)
569.hook: the foolishness of God is wiser than men
569.howItsDone: Catholic churches place a crucifix on or near the altar, Catholics often wear or hang one at home, and on Good Friday the faithful come forward to venerate the cross.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the living sacrifice of Romans 12. Your line was rejoice and weep with them. Whose room did you walk into? Day five hundred sixty-nine.

On the Palatine Hill in Rome, archaeologists found a scratched drawing on an ancient plaster wall. It shows a figure on a cross with the head of a donkey, and a young man raising a hand toward it. Underneath, in rough Greek: Alexamenos worships his god. It's a joke, somebody's mockery of a Christian: the idea of worshiping a crucified man was ridiculous enough to draw. Paul would not have been surprised by it at all.
screen: `A SCRATCH ON A ROMAN WALL.` → `A CRUCIFIED FIGURE, MOCKED.` → `ALEXAMENOS WORSHIPS HIS GOD.`

segments.voice: We're turning now to Paul's letters to Corinth, a rich, proud, quarrelsome port city. The church there is divided, and some members prize clever speech and wisdom. So Paul starts at the hardest point. In the Douay-Rheims: "For the word of the cross, to them indeed that perish, is foolishness; but to them that are saved, that is, to us, it is the power of God." The Greek word for foolishness is moria, folly. Paul is saying: yes, to plenty of listeners, this sounds absurd. A crucified Messiah. A God who wins by losing. Paul knows how it sounds to the people around him. To some, a stumbling block; to others, foolishness. He doesn't make it sound more respectable. Instead he turns it around: "For the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men." Then, with a smile, he tells the Corinthians to look at themselves: not many of you were wise by worldly standards, not many powerful, not many of noble birth. God chose what the world counts foolish and weak. The mocking drawing on the wall and Paul's letter agree on one thing: from the outside, the cross looks absurd. Paul's claim is that the absurd thing is exactly where God chose to show his power. Catholic churches set a crucifix on or near the altar: the very image the mocker drew, now held up without embarrassment.
screen: `CORINTH, PROUD OF ITS WISDOM.` · `MORIA: FOOLISHNESS.` · `A GOD WHO WINS BY LOSING.` · `NOT MANY WISE, NOT MANY MIGHTY.` · then, large: `THE FOOLISHNESS OF GOD IS WISER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one foolish kindness. Settle, and breathe. Think of something kind that would look a little silly or pointless by the world's math. Letting someone have the parking spot. Paying for the coffee behind you. Spending a long time with someone who can't do anything for you. Forgiving a debt, small or large. Picture doing it, and picture someone shaking their head. Let that be fine. If you pray, you can look at a crucifix or picture one, and remember how foolish it looked. The bell holds the time.
The foolishness of the cross. A crucified Messiah, mocked as absurd, and Paul's claim that God's foolishness is wiser than human wisdom. Today's word.
screen: `THE FOOLISHNESS OF THE CROSS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: foolish and wise. Today, do one kind thing that doesn't make sense on paper. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

570.title: God gave the increase (1 Corinthians 3:5–9)
570.howItsDone: Catholics speak of many vocations and gifts serving one Church, priests, religious, catechists, parents and parishioners each with a part, and they pray for growth that they believe comes from God alone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the foolishness of the cross, and a mocking drawing on a Roman wall. Your line was foolish and wise. What foolish kindness did you do? Day five hundred seventy.

Remember Apollos? Eighteen days ago, Priscilla and Aquila took him aside in Ephesus and taught him the way of God more perfectly. Then he crossed to Achaia, Corinth's province, and Acts says he was a great help to the believers there. By the time Paul writes this letter, the church in Corinth has split into fan clubs. Some say, I'm with Paul. Some say, I'm with Apollos. Others, I'm with Cephas, that is, Peter. And some, I'm with Christ. Parishes, teams and families still split this way over favorite people.
screen: `APOLLOS COMES TO CORINTH.` → `I'M WITH PAUL. I'M WITH APOLLOS.` → `A CHURCH OF FAN CLUBS.`

segments.voice: Paul could have used this moment to win. He was the founder, after all. Instead he deflates the whole contest, including himself. Who is Paul, and who is Apollos? he asks. Servants, through whom you believed, each doing what the Lord gave him. Then the picture, in the Douay-Rheims, which spells the name Apollo: "I have planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the increase." A farmer's image. Paul put the seed in the ground in Corinth. Apollos came along later with the watering can. Both mattered. But neither of them can make a seed grow. Growth is not something you can do to a plant; you can only set things up and wait. So, Paul says: "Therefore, neither he that planteth is any thing, nor he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase." That's humbling for the famous preacher, and freeing for everyone else. Then he adds: he who plants and he who waters are one, and each will receive his own reward according to his own labor. Then he widens the picture: "For we are God's coadjutors: you are God's husbandry; you are God's building." Coadjutors means co-workers. Husbandry here means a farm, a field under cultivation. The Corinthians aren't anyone's fan club. They're God's field. Notice how gently Paul treats Apollos. Not a rival, a co-worker. And notice the honest limit of every worker's job. You can't make your kids believe, your friend heal, your project take off, or your parish grow. You plant, you water, and the increase belongs to God. It's a line Catholics reach for when their part seems small.
screen: `WHO IS PAUL? WHO IS APOLLOS?` · `ONE PLANTS, ONE WATERS.` · `ONLY GOD MAKES IT GROW.` · `GOD'S CO-WORKERS.` · then, large: `GOD GAVE THE INCREASE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do your small part. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you care about that you can't control: a child's faith, a friend's recovery, a project at work, a parish, a garden. What's your part in it today? Planting, watering, or simply not trampling it? Name that one small part. Then picture yourself setting down the rest, the growing, which was never yours to do. See if the weight of it lifts a little. If you pray, you can hand God the increase, and keep only your watering can. The bell holds the time.
God gave the increase. Paul planted, Apollos watered, and neither could make anything grow: the growth belongs to God. Today's word.
Your line: god gives the increase. Today, do your one small part well, and let go of the outcome. Day five hundred seventy.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line about teamwork.
what it means: Paul ends a church's fan-club quarrel by saying every worker is a servant, and only God makes anything grow.

what a scholar hears: Paul uses tenses carefully: planted and watered are single past acts, but God was giving the increase all along. and synergoi, co-workers, is the word the Douay-Rheims renders coadjutors.

571.title: A temple (1 Corinthians 6:19–20)
571.hook: your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost
571.howItsDone: Catholics believe the Holy Spirit dwells in the baptized, profess the resurrection of the body in the Creed, and care for the body through rest on Sunday, moderation, and reverence for the bodies of the dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul planting and Apollos watering. Your line was god gives the increase. Did you do your small part, and let go? Day five hundred seventy-one.

A body can be treated like a machine, pushed past every warning light: no sleep, no lunch, one more coffee. Or like a project, to fix, judge, compare and criticize in the mirror. Or, on a good week, like a sturdy thing that simply carries a person through the day. None of these treats it as holy. Corinth had its own version of this argument about the body. And Paul answers it with a startling sentence.
screen: `A MACHINE TO PUSH.` → `A PROJECT TO CRITICIZE.` → `OR: SOMETHING HOLY?`

segments.voice: Some Corinthians, it seems, had a slogan: everything is permitted to me. The body doesn't really matter; it's the spirit that counts. So what you do with your body, in eating, in sex, is spiritually neutral. Paul disagrees, strongly. In the Douay-Rheims: "Or know you not, that your members are the temple of the Holy Ghost, who is in you, whom you have from God; and you are not your own?" To Paul's first readers, a temple was a sacred place. In Jerusalem, the Temple's innermost room was, in Israel's faith, where God's presence dwelt. The Greek word Paul uses here, naos, usually points to the sanctuary itself rather than the whole complex with its courtyards. Paul is saying: the holiest room is you. Your body. Not just your soul. Then: "For you are bought with a great price. Glorify and bear God in your body." Bought with a price: the language of the marketplace, which some readers hear as a slave set free by someone paying. On that reading, not being your own isn't a burden: someone paid a great price. The setting is honest: Paul is warning here about sexual immorality, and he means it seriously. But the reason he gives reaches every part of bodily life. Catholics take this into how they think about the body: it will rise again at the resurrection, the Eucharist is received into it, and it is to be neither worshiped nor despised. Saint John Paul the Second built a whole series of teachings, the theology of the body, on this conviction. A temple isn't a machine or a project. You take care of it, because someone lives there.
screen: `EVERYTHING IS PERMITTED?` · `NAOS: THE INNER SANCTUARY.` · `BOUGHT WITH A PRICE.` · `NOT WORSHIPED, NOT DESPISED.` · then, large: `YOUR BODY IS THE TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest your body today. Settle, and breathe. Start at your feet and move slowly upward. Notice where you're holding tension: jaw, shoulders, the back of the neck. Breathe into each place and let it soften a little. Don't judge anything you find. Just notice, the way you'd walk quietly through a church. Then pick one way to care for your body today: a real meal, a walk, water, going to bed on time. If you pray, you can thank God for the body you have, exactly as it is. The bell holds the time.
A temple. Paul's word for the body: the inner sanctuary where the Holy Spirit lives, bought with a price, and worth caring for. Today's word.
Your line: a temple. Today, give your body one real act of rest or care, as if someone lives there. Day five hundred seventy-one.

572.title: What I received (1 Corinthians 11:23–26)
572.hook: the earliest written account of the Last Supper
572.howItsDone: At every Mass the priest says the words of institution over the bread and the chalice; Catholics kneel, the host and chalice are raised, and in many parishes a bell is rung.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul told the Corinthians that the body is a temple of the Holy Ghost, bought at a price. Your line was a temple. Did you give your body a little rest? Day five hundred seventy-two.

Most scholars think that before Matthew, Mark, Luke or John had set down a single line, a letter crossed the sea from Ephesus to Corinth. Paul had heard something that made him angry. The Christians of Corinth met for the Lord's Supper in a member's house, and it had turned into a dinner party with a cruel side. The well-off ate their fill, and some even got drunk. The poor, perhaps arriving late from work, found nothing left. To correct them, Paul does something nobody had done in writing yet, as far as we know. He sets down the words of the Last Supper.
screen: `A LETTER BEFORE THE GOSPELS.` → `A SUPPER GONE WRONG IN CORINTH.` → `PAUL WRITES DOWN THE LAST SUPPER.`

segments.voice: He opens with a formula, in the Douay-Rheims: "For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you." Received, delivered. In Greek these are the words teachers used for handing on a tradition, the way a student passes on exactly what a teacher said. Paul isn't inventing anything. He's passing along a chain that was already in place, roughly twenty years after the cross. Then come the words themselves. The Lord Jesus, the same night in which he was betrayed, took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and said: "Take ye, and eat: this is my body, which shall be delivered for you: this do for the commemoration of me." Then the cup: the new testament in his blood. In the Greek, one verb is doing double work here. Paul handed on the tradition, and that night Jesus was handed over. Then Paul adds his own line: "For as often as you shall eat this bread, and drink the chalice, you shall shew the death of the Lord, until he come." Every celebration of the supper, he's saying, announces something. That's why the Corinthians' carelessness shocks him. A few verses later he warns that whoever eats and drinks unworthily is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. Catholics read this page as a witness to what happens at every Mass. The priest's words at the consecration come from these accounts, in Paul and in the Gospels, and the Church teaches that the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ. Other Christians understand the supper in other ways, as a spiritual presence or as a memorial, and they reach for this same page. It's very likely the oldest written account we have of words still said at altars every day.
screen: `RECEIVED AND DELIVERED: A TRADITION.` · `THIS IS MY BODY, DELIVERED FOR YOU.` · `YOU SHOW THE LORD'S DEATH.` · `WORDS STILL SAID AT EVERY MASS.` · then, large: `THIS DO FOR THE COMMEMORATION OF ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry Paul's words to the next consecration. If you'll be at Mass this week, wait for the moment the priest lifts the host and then the chalice. Many Catholics silently say Thomas's words then: my Lord and my God. For now, wherever you are, settle and breathe. Picture a table in a house in Corinth, bread broken, a cup passed from hand to hand. Then think of who handed on to you whatever you hold most dear: a faith, a recipe, a way of praying. If you pray, you can say today's line slowly. If you don't, simply remember them with thanks. The bell holds the time.
What I received. Paul's phrase for the words of the Last Supper, handed down to him and handed on to Corinth, written before any Gospel. Today's word.
Your line: I received of the lord. Today, notice one thing someone handed on to you, a habit, a prayer, a story, and pass it on to one person. Day five hundred seventy-two.

573.title: One body (1 Corinthians 12:12–27)
573.hook: the eye can't say to the hand I don't need you
573.howItsDone: Catholics speak of the Church as the Mystical Body of Christ; at Mass the bidding prayers bring the needs of the sick, the absent and the whole Church before the parish as members of one body.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul wrote down the words of the Last Supper, the oldest written account we have. Your line was I received of the lord. What did you hand on? Day five hundred seventy-three.

Corinth had a healing shrine to the Greek god Asclepius, and people who believed they'd been cured left clay models of the part that got better: a hand, a foot, an ear, an eye. Archaeologists have dug them up there. Some scholars wonder whether Paul's readers thought of those shelves of separate clay limbs when they heard today's chapter. Because the church in Corinth was falling into pieces. People with showy gifts felt important. Quiet people felt they didn't count. Paul answers with a body, and not a pile of parts.
screen: `CLAY HANDS AND FEET IN CORINTH.` → `WHOSE GIFT MATTERS MOST?` → `PAUL ANSWERS WITH A BODY.`

segments.voice: His picture is simple enough for a child. The body has many members, and all of them together are one body. Then he gives the parts voices. The foot says: because I am not the hand, I am not of the body. Or the ear sulking because it isn't an eye. If the whole body were an eye, he asks, where would the hearing be? Then he turns to the ones who feel superior: "And the eye cannot say to the hand: I need not thy help; nor again the head to the feet: I have no need of you." In fact, he says, the members that seem weaker are necessary, and we give the less honored parts more care. If one member suffers, all suffer with it. If one is honored, all rejoice. Then the line it's all been building to: "Now you are the body of Christ, and members of member." The image wasn't new. The Roman historian Livy tells an old fable of the limbs and the belly, used to persuade the common people to go back to serving the city's rulers. Paul uses the body the other way round, to give the weaker parts more honor. Catholics read this chapter as one of the roots of a central teaching: the Church is the Mystical Body of Christ, with Christ as the head and the faithful as the members. Pope Pius the Twelfth wrote a whole encyclical on it in 1943. It's why Catholics speak of a parish in Lagos and a parish in Ohio as one body, not two clubs, and why the housebound person praying a rosary at home counts as a working member. In this body, nobody is spare.
screen: `MANY MEMBERS, ONE BODY.` · `THE EYE CAN'T SAY: I NEED NOT THY HELP.` · `THE WEAKER PARTS GET MORE HONOR.` · `THE MYSTICAL BODY OF CHRIST.` · then, large: `NOW YOU ARE THE BODY OF CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the hand you need. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose gift is nothing like yours. If you're a talker, a listener. If you're a planner, someone who just shows up and fixes things. Maybe someone you've quietly thought you could do without. Picture them clearly. Now notice what would fall apart if they weren't there: at work, at home, in your parish. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. Either way, decide how you'll thank them in person today, and what you'll say. The bell holds the time.
One body. Paul's picture of the Church: many members, every one of them needed, and together the body of Christ. Today's word.
Your line: the hand needs the eye. Today, thank one person whose gift is different from yours, and name the gift out loud. Day five hundred seventy-three.

574.title: Charity is patient (1 Corinthians 13:1–7)
574.hook: charity is patient, is kind, envieth not
574.howItsDone: Catholics count charity as one of the three theological virtues with faith and hope, and 1 Corinthians 13 is one of the readings couples may choose for a Catholic wedding.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the eye and the hand, and one body with no spare parts. Your line was the hand needs the eye. Who did you thank, and for what gift? Day five hundred seventy-four.

It's often read at weddings, so it's easy to assume it was written for one. It wasn't. Paul was writing to a church that was quarreling: over which leader to follow, over food, over who had the most impressive spiritual gift. Right in the middle of his argument about gifts, he stops. I'll show you, he says, a more excellent way. And then he writes the passage that has long outlived the quarrel.
screen: `WRITTEN FOR A WEDDING?` → `NO: FOR A CHURCH IN A FIGHT.` → `A MORE EXCELLENT WAY.`

segments.voice: He begins by making every gift worthless without it: "If I speak with the tongues of men, and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal." Then he describes charity, and notice he doesn't describe a feeling. He lists what it does and what it won't do: "Charity is patient, is kind: charity envieth not, dealeth not perversely; is not puffed up." It isn't ambitious, doesn't seek its own, isn't provoked to anger, thinks no evil. Then four alls: "Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things." Why does the Douay-Rheims say charity and not love? Paul's Greek word is agapē. Saint Jerome's Latin Bible rendered it caritas, and the Douay-Rheims followed the Latin. So, here, did the King James. Newer English translations tend to say love. In everyday English, charity has shrunk to mean giving money. In Catholic teaching it keeps the old, large meaning. The Catechism calls charity the virtue by which we love God above all things for his own sake, and our neighbor as ourselves for the love of God. Some readers try a simple exercise: read the passage again with their own name where it says charity. Patient, kind, not puffed up. The first line is the hard one. And that first line matters. Of everything Paul could have put first, he put patience.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse patience. Settle, and breathe. Think of the place you're most likely to lose patience today. A slow line. A child who won't put on shoes. A coworker who explains the same thing twice. Picture it happening, and notice whatever starts to rise. Now picture yourself waiting it out, one breath longer than usual, and saying nothing sharp. Just once. If you pray, you can say the line charity is patient, is kind, slowly, as a prayer. If you don't, just rest in that one longer breath. The bell holds the time.
Charity. The Douay-Rheims word for Paul's agapē: love that gives itself. The first thing he says it is: patient. Today's word.

Your line: charity is patient. Today, be patient once on purpose, and notice it. And that's week eighty-two: a living sacrifice, the foolishness of the cross, God gave the increase, a temple, what I received, one body, and charity. Day five hundred seventy-four.

original.note: Greek: love. rendered caritas in Jerome's Latin, and charity in the Douay-Rheims.

trapdoor: what you thought: charity means giving money.
what it means: in Paul and in Catholic teaching, charity is love itself, the patient, kind love of God and neighbor.
what a scholar hears: agapē, rendered caritas by Jerome; the English word kept the Latin, then shrank in everyday use to almsgiving.
